newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU holds back on escalating chicken trade war.
newsitem.headline: EU holds back on escalating chicken trade war.

text.p: The European Union has no plans to escalate the trade war with the United States over meat imports, at least for the moment, a European Commission spokesman said on Wednesday.
"At the moment our objective is to conclude an agreement" in the transatlantic dispute over meat inspection procedures, the spokesman said.
The row blew up into a fully fledged trade fight on Tuesday as Washington acted to cut off imports of European Union meat, and the EU effectively halted incoming shipments of U.S. poultry.
Asked specificaly if the Commission was considering counter measures following the U.S. action, the spokesman said "No. We are still negotiating. The U.S. has not introduced the measures yet."
The U.S. measures, which would block an estimated $300 million of imports of EU meat, mainly Danish ham, are only due to come into force on April 15.

The spokesman called the planned American action "totally disproportionate" as EU curbs on imports of U.S. chicken meat and dairy products would only affect an estimated $100 million dollars of exports annually.

Sparking the blow-up was the inability of U.S. and EU officials to settle an old dispute over meat import inspection standards. Agreement on the so-called veterinary equivalency issue would allow each side to accept meat and poultry products from the other even if inspection methods differ.

Negotiators had worked all last week to beat an April 1 deadline by which the EU said it would implement new inspection standards for U.S. poultry shipments that the American industry says are unfair and cannot be met.
Washington had warned it would play hardball if the EU took such action, and on Tuesday both sides lived up to their threats.
As promised, the EU imposed new rules throughout its 15 member nations that would require U.S. poultry and meat exporters to meet European inspection standards.
Affected almost immediately will be some $100 million worth of U.S. poultry, dairy and egg shipments normally sold to the EU.
Paul Drazek, senior trade advisor at the Agriculture Department, said the United States would no longer provide export certificates for the shipments because of the new rules.
Washington quickly slapped the EU with new requirements for meat imports from the EU.

Under a new system, over 100 European meat and poultry packing and processing plants will now have to meet U.S. inspection standards. U.S. officials said most of these plants would probably be taken off the Agriculture Department's approved list of exporters in the next few days.
